body.objective: Students will be able to count 6/8 and 9/8.
successCriteria: I can count and feel 6/8 and 9/8 in two or three big beats
I can tell simple metre from compound metre
I can perform music that changes metre
body.hook: Try counting "1-2-3, 4-5-6" while marching: it feels like galloping. That's compound metre. And if you've ever heard the "Mission: Impossible" theme, you've heard 5/4, a metre that feels like it's missing a step.

vocabulary.definition: A metre where each beat divides into two (2/4, 3/4, 4/4).
A metre where each beat divides into three (6/8, 9/8, 12/8).
In compound metre, the beat is a dotted quarter note (three eighths).
Music where the time signature changes during the piece.
A metre with uneven beat groupings, such as 5/4 or 7/8.
The shape a conductor draws to show the beats in a bar.

study.title: Feeling in Threes
study.question: How do musicians count and feel compound and mixed metres?
study.passage:
Part 1, Simple vs compound (10 minutes): 3/4 = three quarter-note beats, each dividing in two ("1 & 2 & 3 &"). 6/8 = six eighth notes grouped 3 + 3, felt as two dotted-quarter beats ("1-la-li 2-la-li"). Count both aloud while clapping. They have the same number of eighths but feel totally different.
Part 2, 9/8 and 12/8 (10 minutes): 9/8 = three dotted-quarter beats (3 + 3 + 3); 12/8 = four (3 + 3 + 3 + 3), the shuffle feel in blues.
Part 3, Asymmetric (10 minutes): 5/4 grouped 3 + 2 ("1 2 3 1 2"); 7/8 grouped 2 + 2 + 3 or 3 + 2 + 2. Clap the accents.
Part 4, Conducting (5 minutes): Conduct 6/8 in two, 9/8 in three.
Part 5, Mixed metre etude (15 minutes): Play a short exercise that changes 4/4, 6/8, 5/4, 4/4. Rule: in many band pieces the eighth note stays the same speed across changes; check the marking (for example eighth = eighth).
study.source: Original rhythm workshop written for this lesson.
discussion: Why do 3/4 and 6/8 feel different with the same number of eighths?

study.product: Perform a mixed-metre etude accurately and write a counting guide for four bars that change between simple, compound and asymmetric metres.

items.q: Define compound metre.
items.answer: A metre where each beat divides into three.

items.q: How many eighths are in 9/8?
Explain why 6/8 is usually felt in two.
items.answer: Six eighths group into two sets of three, making two dotted-quarter beats.

items.q: Give two possible groupings for 7/8.
What does the conducting pattern for 9/8 look like?
What is the difference between 3/4 and 6/8?
items.answer: 3/4 is three beats dividing in two; 6/8 is two beats dividing in three.

items.q: Explain how you would count through a change from 4/4 to 6/8 with eighth = eighth.
items.answer: Keep the eighth steady; switch from groups of two to groups of three.

items.q: Explain why composers use asymmetric metres.
items.answer: To create uneven, energetic or surprising rhythmic feels.
